content.overview: Seed propagation creates genetically distinct offspring, so specialist work begins with identity, provenance, lot context and the distinction between seed identity and clonal identity.

sections.title: Seed identity is not genotype identity
sections.body: A seed lot can be traceable to a cross, cultivar or production lot without every resulting seedling being genetically identical. Sexual reproduction preserves parentage information while segregation and recombination create within-family variation.

sections.title: Record provenance before treatment
sections.body: Lot ID, source, production date when known, storage history, seed count and any pre-treatment belong in the record before germination begins. Missing provenance reduces the interpretability of later performance.

sections.title: Anatomy supports observation
sections.body: The seed coat, embryo axis, cotyledons and emerging radicle provide practical landmarks for distinguishing imbibition, radicle emergence and seedling establishment.

commonMistakes: Treating a research protocol value as a universal production target.
Reporting successful seedlings without preserving the original denominator.
Changing multiple variables at once and then claiming one caused the result.
content.practicalApplication: Audit a mock seed lot and identify which fields are required to reconstruct source, count, storage context and treatment history.
content.summary: Use source-controlled evidence, preserve identity and denominators, and keep observations separate from explanations.
